1:
No question has been asked, so the word answered needs accounting for. The Gloss says he was meeting their evil thoughts of putting him to death. Henry says the same at more length: his opposers had been put to silence, so he answered not their words but their thoughts, while they were wishing for an opportunity to lay hands on him — Christ knows how to answer men’s thoughts, being a discerner of them — though Henry allows the alternative, that he simply continued the same discourse under another figure. Ellicott takes the word to imply a connection of some kind with what went before, an answer if not to spoken words then to the thoughts stirring in his hearers. Wesley says he spoke with reference to what had just passed. Chrysostom and John Chrysostom both find the connection in the sentence just uttered, that the kingdom should be given to a nation bringing forth the fruits of it: he now proceeds to show what nation that is. John Chrysostom adds what the new parable contributes beyond the last. It marks the difference between the Son and the servants; it foretells the casting out of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles; it indicates the strictness of life required and the punishment awaiting the careless; and it is well placed after the other, since in the earlier parable he is bidding them before his crucifixion, while here he still urges them after he has been slain, pressing men to the marriage who had deserved the most grievous punishment. Gill notes that the audience was not the multitude only but the chief priests, elders, scribes and Pharisees, and that though one Gospel seems to say the rulers withdrew, the Pharisees at least remained to hear it.

Whether this is the same parable Luke records is the first real question. Augustine states flatly that it is related only by Matthew, and that Luke gives one like it which is not the same, as the order shows. Gregory allows more accommodation. He distinguishes the two by their subjects — the wedding feast here means the present Church, into which some enter who shall perish, while the supper there means the last and eternal feast, from which whoever has once entered shall never be put out — but adds that if anyone maintains they are the same lesson, the difference may be explained by Matthew having related the episode of the guest without a garment which Luke omits, and by the ancient custom which put dinner at the ninth hour, so that the one meal might fairly be called by either name. Robertson reports the modern form of the same dispute and refuses it. Some hold that this is merely Matthew’s version of Luke’s parable, misplaced through his habit of grouping sayings; that, he says, is a gratuitous indictment of a report which locates the parable here by an explicit again. Others hold that Jesus never spoke it at all, and that the writer composed it to cover the sin and fate of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles; but it is like Jesus and suits the present occasion. Calvin goes the other way and treats them as one discourse differently placed. Luke does not specify a time while Matthew expressly affirms that Christ delivered it here, so Calvin follows Matthew’s order, observing that the evangelist’s design was to show what roused the scribes to fury and that he therefore set it among the discourses they most hated without regard to chronology; but he still attends to Luke’s account of what prompted it, and judges that the guest at the Pharisee’s table who exclaimed about eating bread in the kingdom spoke neither from piety nor in mockery, but as men of moderate knowledge and no open wickedness will talk idly of eternal life over their cups.
2:
Barnes reads the opening formula loosely: God deals with men under the gospel as a certain king did, and the parable as a whole refers to the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles, with many circumstances thrown in to fill out the narrative that cannot be particularly explained. On the marriage he, Robertson and Clarke agree that the word means a feast rather than the ceremony; Robertson adds that the plural used here is the ordinary papyrus term for wedding festivities, which ran seven days in the story of Samson, and that the exact phrase turns up in the Doric of Thera about 200 B.C. Clarke offers a second sense, a feast of inauguration held when a son was put in possession of the government, so that he and his new subjects became married together, and points to Adonijah and Solomon for the custom. He then lays out the key: the king is God, the son is Christ, the marriage his taking of human nature into union with himself, the feast the economy of the gospel, and those bidden the Jews, invited by all the prophets. He also notes rabbinic parables in Bereshith Rabba and the Sohar closely similar to this one, which he thinks vastly ennobled by passing through the hands of our Lord. Gill says only that the design is to express the great love of God the Father. Ellicott traces the image further back, to prophets who spoke of God as bridegroom and Israel as bride and of her idolatry as the adultery of a faithless wife, and observes that this is the first place the figure appears fully developed, the germ being a passing allusion elsewhere in Luke. He enters one caution: the wedding is between Christ and his Church, so the guests, in their collective unity, are themselves the bride — a truth the form of the parable has to exclude. Wesley compresses the verse into a line about God bringing his first-begotten into the world.

The servants and their errand divide the readings. Gill takes them for the ministers of the gospel, of God’s own choosing, calling and qualifying, who serve him willingly, and suggests John the Baptist and the twelve. Clarke agrees on the Baptist but pairs him with the seventy. Ellicott takes them instead for the aggregate work of the prophets down to the Baptist. Barnes and Robertson both fasten on the double summons. Barnes finds two invitations, one well beforehand so that guests might prepare, the second to give notice of the precise hour; Robertson supplies the Jewish custom of inviting a second time those already invited, cites Esther for it, and points out a play on words in the Greek, to call the called, which he credits to Vincent and says both the Authorised and Revised Versions lose. Calvin describes the same custom from the host’s side, a list drawn up of intended guests and servants afterwards sent to them, and reads the two stages as a double favour: Israel preferred to other nations, then told of its adoption by the prophets. He opens with a Spartan’s word about the Athenians, that they knew what was right and would not practise it, and grants without objection the common view that the son’s marriage means God’s design to make Christ governor of his people and unite the Church to him. On the refusal Ellicott concedes that it looks improbable, and answers that it is natural enough in subjects rebellious at heart, which is exactly the character the parable was drawn to portray. Robertson calls the negative imperfect a settled refusal and borrows Conder’s phrase, the Hebrew tragedy. Barnes turns it on the reader: they might have come if they chose, and every difficulty a sinner labours under lies in the will.
4:
The second embassy is read by everyone as the nearer and more urgent call. Gill assigns it to the seventy and the later gospel ministers, Barnabas and Saul among them, preaching to the Jews before the destruction of Jerusalem. Barnes puts it simply, that God repeats his message to sinners when they reject it. Calvin makes the point turn on the one body of the people: the same nation is addressed throughout, the first invitation covering all the prophecies down to the gospel, and this second arriving at the very hour. He then observes an escalation. Of the ancient people Christ charges nothing worse than contempt and pride, but the servants sent last were killed; the nation reached the highest pitch of its crimes when haughty rejection was followed by the madness of cruelty. Even under the gospel call, he adds, some ridiculed grace as careless despisers while hypocrites furiously rejected it, and he takes it for a rule that ungodly men rage against God the more fiercely in proportion to the earnestness with which he invites them.

The word rendered dinner produces a three-cornered philological disagreement. Barnes grants that it literally denotes the meal taken about noon, but argues that since eastern marriages were held in the evening it must here mean an evening meal. Ellicott says the Greek points rather to a morning meal as against the evening supper, and adds that such words drift, being food taken at sunrise in Homer and the repast of noon in later authors. Robertson is blunt that it is breakfast and not dinner, notes that Luke uses both words side by side, and untangles the confusion: the midday meal was sometimes called a midday supper, the real supper came in the evening, and once the earlier term had shifted to luncheon another word was needed for the first meal of the day. On the fatlings there is more agreement. Clarke makes them fatted rams or wethers, Wesley fatted beasts and fowls, Robertson derives the word from a verb meaning to fatten with grain, and Barnes declines to fix a species, allowing only that since oxen are named separately these are likely lambs or calves. Ellicott hears behind the killed oxen an imagery Isaiah had used, and reads the provision as the peace and joy Christ came to offer.

Then the two refusals. Barnes distinguishes them sharply: one part treated the invitation with silent contempt and coolly went about its business, while the rest were not satisfied with that but showed positive malignity — some sinners are content merely to neglect religion, others attack it with open violence. Robertson is careful that the verb says only neglecting, not caring for; they may have ridiculed the invitation but the word does not say so, though to neglect such a summons is a gross discourtesy. Ellicott sees one temper of neglect that slights the kingdom and prefers this world, and a second running parallel with it and passing on into open antagonism. Gill treats the imprisonment of the servants as the arrest of Peter and John soon after the ascension, while Ellicott holds that the parable here looks forward as well as back, taking in the sufferings of Christian preachers and martyrs alongside those of the prophets. Calvin is least interested in the violent party and most in the farm and the merchandise. Men created for a heavenly life are so carried away after transitory things that hardly one in a hundred prefers the kingdom of God, and the excuse of lawful business is exactly what Christ takes from us: the conveniences of this life are given to draw us to God, yet marriage and fields and riches become snares binding men closer to the earth. Wesley says it in a sentence: one must mind what he has and another gain what he wants, and how many perish by misusing lawful things.
7:
Nobody hesitates over the burning of the city. Barnes takes it for the Jews and Jerusalem — they were murderers, having slain the prophets, and God was about to send the armies of Rome under his providential direction. Wesley says the same in half a line, the Roman armies employed of God, and the murderers primarily the Jews. Ellicott adds a second horizon: as in other parables shadowing the judgment of the Son of Man, the words find an approximate fulfilment first in the destruction of Jerusalem and afterwards in every trouble that falls on nations and churches as the punishment of unbelief. Two of them shrink the scale of the word rendered armies. Robertson makes them bands of soldiers, not grand armies; Ellicott says the modern sense suggests action on a larger scale than the Greek indicates and prefers troops. Clarke leaves the sense alone and reports a variant instead: he reads this very king, on the authority of nine of the most ancient manuscripts and nearly a hundred others, the later Syriac, six copies of the Itala and some of the fathers, noting that several printed editions carry it and that Griesbach took it into the text. Calvin observes that the punishment is in this Gospel alone, Luke reporting no outrage on the servants at all, though both agree that those who did not come at the appointed time were shut out; and he refuses to leave it with the Jews, since the same destruction awaits all the ungodly who violently oppose the ministers of the gospel, and those so occupied with earthly cares as to set no value on the divine invitation will perish at length in famine and want.

On the unworthiness Clarke brings in an argument from custom. Among the Mohammedans, refusing an invitation to a marriage feast is reckoned a breach of the law of God, and he quotes two authorities to that effect; he supposes the same held across the oriental nations, and says the observation is needed to show how grave the refusal in the text really was. His own definition of worthiness is the opposite of desert: a man is fit for this feast when, feeling his wretchedness and misery, he comes to God in the appointed way to get entrance by the blood of Jesus. Gill notes only that the servants now addressed are those preserved from the rage of their enemies, who outlived them and saw their ruin.
9:
The highways are read topographically and then theologically. Barnes makes the word the going out of the paths, the principal street into which smaller ones empty, a place of confluence where people of all descriptions are found; Clarke and Ellicott alike make it the point where two or more roads meet, and Robertson distinguishes the double compound from the simple word for cross-streets, taking it for main roads leading out of the city with side-turnings off them. Clarke adds that Luke supplies hedges, which points to miserable vagabonds and the indigent poor sitting by the wayside imploring relief, and that a rich man making a feast would go out and invite destitute travellers. Lightfoot documents the same practice from the rabbis, both the custom of inviting poor travellers and the order of sitting, the travellers coming in and taking benches until all the invited had arrived. All then read the Gentiles here. Barnes says they were commonly regarded by Jews as living in highways and hedges, cast out and despised; Gill calls them far off, walking in their own ways; Ellicott finds the apt illustration in Paul at Pisidian Antioch, turning from Jews who counted themselves unworthy of eternal life; Clarke draws the widest conclusion, that God sends his salvation to every soul that all may believe and be saved. Calvin argues it from the Song of Moses, that the calling of a foolish nation was designed to provoke Israel to jealousy, and from the wild branches grafted into the olive; and he turns the warning on the reader, that the same punishment will fall on us if we do not answer the call, for the supper will not be lost — God will invite other guests.

That the gathering is of bad and good is taken by three of them as the mixed state of the visible Church. Clarke lists the figures for it: the floor where wheat and chaff lie together, the field with its bastard wheat, the net that collects of all kinds, the house of wise and foolish, the fold of sheep and goats. Ellicott makes the same comparison with the drag-net and draws two things from it, the universality of the offer, so that no previous sin shuts a man out, and a company waiting for the King to come in and see the guests. Barnes is sharper: all descriptions of people, and none of them good by nature, since if they were they would not need the gospel, though some are worse than others and have special need of it. Wesley says it in four words, by preaching everywhere. Robertson and Ellicott close on a variant, that some early manuscripts read the bride-chamber rather than the wedding; Robertson thinks the marriage dining hall rightly read there, while Ellicott suspects an explanatory note that crept into the text.
11:
The inspection first. Ellicott notes that the verb carries the sense of inspecting: the king came to see whether the guests had met the condition implied in the invitation. Gill reads the visit as the omniscience of God over professors of religion, distinguishing hypocrites from real believers — sometimes by gracious visits to his own, sometimes in providence against formal professors, and finally at the last judgment. Clarke states that plainly as the day God comes to judge the world. On the garment itself the historical case is built by three of them together. Barnes recalls that kings made presents of raiment to favourites, that refusing them expressed the highest contempt, and that the host of a feast prepared the long white robes his guests were to wear; this man came in his common dress, as taken from the highway, though one had been provided if he had applied for it. Ellicott supposes the same custom and adds that wardrobes of many thousand garments were part of an Eastern prince’s wealth, brought out on state occasions as when Jehu assembled the worshippers of Baal. Clarke adds Zephaniah’s threat against all clothed with strange apparel, and two customs from outside Scripture: Homer’s Telemachus, bathed, anointed and clothed in fresh mantles at a wedding feast in Lacedaemon, and the caftans an Asiatic nobleman keeps by the wardrobe-full for those he honours, refusal to wear them being the highest insult. Ellicott then blocks one inference: nothing may be drawn from there being a single offender, any more than from the single wicked servant in the parable of the Talents.

What the garment is divides them, and Ellicott states the alternatives before rejecting them. Some have taken it for the outward ordinance of baptism, some for the imputed righteousness of Christ covering the nakedness of our own; both answers he judges at once too narrow and too technical, preferring the analogy of scriptural symbolism, in which a man’s garment stands for the habits of good or evil by which his character is shown, so that the wedding garment is nothing less than the holiness without which no man shall see the Lord, which Christ is ready to impart to whoever truly believes. Clarke lands in the same place and underlines it word by word: holiness of heart and life, the fine white linen being the righteousness of the saints — righteousness meaning the whole external conduct regulated by the will and word of God, and saints meaning those whose souls were purified by the blood of the Lamb. Wesley, in one line, takes the position Ellicott has just set aside, calling it the righteousness of Christ first imputed and then implanted, and notes that the verse has no relation to the Lord’s Supper but to God’s proceeding at the last day. Barnes speaks in the same idiom, a garment of salvation wrought by the Saviour’s hands and dyed in his blood, against which the hypocrite prefers the filthy rags of his own righteousness. Calvin calls the question — faith, or a holy life? — a useless controversy, since faith cannot be separated from good works nor good works proceed from any other source than faith; Christ meant only that God calls us on the express condition of being renewed by the Spirit after his image. He also answers an objection the others do not raise: how can a beggar be punished so severely for lacking a garment, when men who beg on the roads are expected to go in rags? The question is not how it is procured, for whomever the Lord invites he clothes, finding in us nothing but nakedness and filth and adorning us with magnificent attire. And he presses the warning where the Jews are not: Christ is now cautioning those put into their room, since not all who have once entered the Church partake of everlasting life.
12:
At the confrontation Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott agree on both words. Friend is better rendered companion, the Greek not implying friendship; Clarke says the man may be called a companion because he is a member of the visible Church present at every ordinance, and reads the question as asking why he professed the king’s name while living unprepared for his kingdom. Gill allows the address to be either ironical or a concession to his profession. On speechless, Barnes says simply that he had no excuse, and so it will be with all hypocrites; Clarke and Ellicott both give the literal force, muzzled or gagged, Ellicott noting it is the same verb used later of the Sadducees being put to silence. Clarke then turns the case into an argument. If this man is by general consent the emblem of those who perish at the last day, where does absolute reprobation appear in him? Had Christ never died for him, or had he asked for the garment and been refused, he might have pleaded it and the just God would have listened; but Christ died for him, the ministers invited him, the Spirit strove with him, and he is condemned not for lacking what he could not get but for lacking what he might have had. Robertson stays with the grammar and with a report of the scholarship: some hold this scene a fragment of a lost parable separate from the wedding feast, for which he finds no evidence, and he relays a rabbinic story of a king who named no hour, so that the guests who dressed and waited went in while those who went off to work were made to stand and watch. Cyril of Jerusalem uses the verse pastorally on candidates for baptism, telling them to wash their robes in repentance so as to be found clean when called to the bride-chamber, since the Bridegroom invites all without distinction but afterwards separates those who have come in.

The sentence itself draws a textual note and a scene-painting. Ellicott reports that take him away is wanting in many of the best manuscripts and may have been inserted to relieve the difficulty of a man simply thrust out after being bound hand and foot. On the outer darkness he, Barnes and Robertson all point back to the same phrase earlier in this Gospel; Barnes takes it without doubt for the future punishment of the hypocrite, while Ellicott and Robertson both draw the force from the contrast — a bridal chamber with its lights and mirth and music, and the midnight blackness outside the palace, all the blacker for the brilliance within, filled with the groans of the excluded. Clarke supplies the custom behind the image, that Jewish marriages were held at night in a hall superbly illuminated, so that the darkness outside was made more gloomy still to a man suddenly thrust into it from such a profusion of light. Gill is alone in asking who the servants are that carry out the sentence: either the ministers and pastors who by Christ’s order cast out those whose principles and practices show them to be without grace, or, as he prefers, the angels who bind the tares in bundles and sever the wicked from the just.
14:
The closing maxim is treated by everyone as a summary, but they differ over what it summarises. Barnes is the most explicit and the most restrictive: the remark is drawn from the whole parable and not from the episode of the garment, so it does not mean that the mass inside the church are merely called and not chosen, but that the mass of the human family in Christ’s day had been called and had rejected the mercy of God. He grants the other applications — the Jews were called and few chosen to life, nation after nation has been called and few have shown themselves the elect of God, and many in the church may prove at last to be without the garment — but he will not let the sentence be read off the last scene alone. Clarke and Wesley read it exactly that way. Clarke takes the called for those brought by the preaching into the outward communion of the Church, and the chosen for the few who will dwell with God in glory, the rest never having come to the master of the feast for a garment; he illustrates it from the Roman levy, where all were mustered but only the fit taken, and charges the reader to examine his soul and make sure work for eternity. Wesley compresses it into two clauses: many hear, few believe; many belong to the visible Church and few to the invisible. Clarke notes too that the verse is missing from one manuscript collated by Griesbach.

How much doctrine of election the saying will carry is the second question, and the two who might be expected to press it hardest both decline. Calvin says the object of the parable is pointed out by its conclusion, from which he infers that we should not press every clause; a moment ago Christ threatened one man only, and now we learn that out of a large number few will be retained. Though the gospel gathers more into the Church than the law did, only a small portion prove their faith by newness of life, so no one should flatter himself with the empty title of faith. Then he stops deliberately: he will enter no further into the question of God’s eternal election, because Christ’s words mean only that an external profession is no proof that God will own all who appear to have ranged themselves under his banner. Ellicott stops at the same line from the other side. The calling answers, verbally and in substance, to the bidding of the parable, and the chosen are those who accept the invitation and comply with its condition; so far as the parable goes, the choice depends on the answer given to the call. Election according to the foreknowledge of God is not within view here, though it follows once that foreknowledge is assumed, and the choice that closes the story must have been present to the mind of the All-knowing from eternity. He warns as well against fixing time limits on the thoughts of God. Robertson keeps to the wording: the saying turns up in several connections, since Christ repeated himself as every teacher does, and the two terms are not equivalents, the chosen being called out from among the called.

Origen puts the saying to a use none of the others attempt, as a reply to an objection. Someone may point, to shame him, at the number of church members thought to believe; the answer is not only that many are called and few chosen, but the charge to strive to enter by the narrow door, since many will seek and not be able. Behind that stands a stricter definition of what a church is: a soul with spot or wrinkle, neither holy nor blameless, is not a rock on which Christ builds, nor a church, nor part of one.
15:
The change of tactics is what strikes them first. John Chrysostom fastens on the word then and asks when: at the very moment they should have been moved to compunction, amazed at his love and sobered by seeing the parables fulfilled in fact. Yet their wicked acts do not cease but go further; unable to lay hands on him for fear of the multitude, they took another way, meaning to make him guilty of crimes against the state. Pseudo-Chrysostom gives the same movement as an image: dam a running stream and it cuts a new channel, and so their malevolence, foiled on one side, seeks out another course. Gill fixes the moment more precisely: the Pharisees had stayed to hear the parable of the marriage feast and saw themselves designed in it; provoked past bearing but unable to use violence for fear of the people, they withdrew to a council chamber or the high priest’s palace, where the chief priests had gone. Henry sets it in the day’s sequence: the encounters so far had been with chief priests and elders, men in authority who trusted more to power than to policy and had challenged his commission, and now he is set upon from another quarter, the Pharisees trying whether learning in the law can do what force could not. It was not the least of Christ’s sufferings, he adds, that he endured the contradiction of sinners.

On took counsel Henry presses the deliberation itself. It was foretold that the rulers would take counsel against him, and so they had persecuted the prophets, saying come and let us devise devices against Jeremiah; the more contrivance goes into a sin the worse it is, and the more wicked wit in the contriving, the more wicked will in the committing. He draws the lesson too that no ingenuity or integrity screens a man from the strife of tongues. Robertson notes the phrase is a Latinism.

The word for entangle is worked over by four of them, who arrive at one picture. Barnes explains that to entangle is to ensnare as birds are taken by a net, by leading them within its compass and springing it over them, so that here it means to lay a plan for enticing and to beguile by a question that may draw an incautious answer. Robertson traces the verb to the noun for a snare, observes that it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and calls it a vivid picture of tripping Jesus in his speech like a bird or a wild beast. Ellicott says the phrase is exactly our colloquial set a trap, and infers that they dared not move against him openly while popular feeling stood where it did. Barnes adds that the possessive in his talk was supplied by the translators, perhaps wrongly, since the phrase means in conversation and alludes to nothing he had said before. Clarke reads the phrase as by discourse, and states plainly what the trap was for: subtle questions whose answers might involve him either with the Roman government or with the great Sanhedrin.

Calvin alone reconstructs the political ground under the plan. Having failed in everything else, they judged the quickest way to destroy him was to have him taken for a seditious person, and the tribute was the readiest matter, a great dispute running among the Jews over it. The Romans had claimed for themselves the payment which the law of Moses reserved for God, so that men complained it was an intolerable crime for profane rulers to seize a divine prerogative; and since that payment had been a testimony of their adoption they reckoned themselves robbed of an honour justly theirs. The poorer a man was, the bolder to raise sedition. Their principal object, he adds, was to make the people dislike him; they supposed him now so surrounded that he could no longer escape.
16:
Who the Herodians were is the largest question here, and the accounts do not agree. Robertson says flatly that they were neither kinsmen of Herod nor his soldiers but partisans, the ending of the name being a Latin termination like that in Christians. Jerome says just as flatly that they were Herod’s soldiers, or else men the Pharisees called Herodians in mockery because they paid tribute to Rome and were not devoted to the worship of God; Clarke reports that the Syriac makes them Herod’s domestics. Ellicott observes that they are known to us only through two Gospels, that the form of the name is Latin like Pompeiani and shows the influence of that language in Palestinian public life, and that two theories hold the field: either they were adherents of the Herodian house who therefore held tribute lawful, so that two opposed parties are here coalescing against a common enemy, or they looked to the Herods to restore national independence and agreed with the Pharisees on tribute while differing on all else. Barnes takes the first view from Prideaux: the law forbade setting a stranger over Israel as king, but Herod held that this bound only a voluntary choice and not a submission forced by conquest, so tribute to a foreign prince was lawful. Wesley says the same in a sentence: attachment to Herod made them zealous for the Roman government that upheld his family’s dignity. Lightfoot and Ellicott independently trace the party to one incident: Menahem, Hillel’s colleague at the head of the council, withdrew into Herod’s service with eighty men gorgeously clad, and those who got into the court took the name. Lightfoot adds that they held the Sadducean doctrine and had leavened Herod with it, which is why what one Gospel calls the leaven of the Sadducees another calls the leaven of Herod; Barnes notes the pairing and makes their second tenet the lawfulness of adopting a conqueror’s religious usages. Jerome sets the quarrel in its history: Judaea was made tributary at the census under Augustus, and the people were divided, some holding tribute owed for the security Roman arms maintained, while the Pharisees, satisfied in their own righteousness, contended that a people who paid tithes and firstfruits owed nothing to human laws.

The compliment is read by all as calculated. Gill notes that the Pharisees sent disciples rather than come themselves, choosing the craftiest and best trained, who might pass unrecognised and whose air of simplicity would look like sincerity. Clarke grants that the words were true — this was our Lord’s real character — and that is what makes them damning: they testify to the truth only to make it serve their purpose, for men moved by the wicked one never do good except when they hope to accomplish evil by it, and he concludes that men who praise you to your face are always to be suspected. Gloss analyses the flattery as a checklist. There are three ways a man may fail to teach truth — not knowing or not loving it, suppressing what he knows of God for want of fear, or withholding it from his neighbour through fear or affection — and each of their clauses shuts off one. Calvin turns the same clauses into a definition of the faithful teacher they pretended to think him: one who does not introduce the contrivances of men or depart from the pure word, who gives out with his hands what he learned from the mouth of God, and who fits his teaching to the people’s edification without disguising it; against which he sets Paul’s hucksters, who do not openly overturn sound doctrine but corrupt its purity out of ambition or covetousness. Robertson takes the last clause literally, that Christ regards not the face of men, identifies it with the partiality James condemns, and adds that the flattery implied Jesus was a reckless simpleton.
17:
On the question itself Barnes explains that the tribute is the tax paid to Rome and that Caesar had become a common name for every emperor as Pharaoh was for the kings of Egypt, the one then reigning being Tiberius. Ellicott is more precise: the word is the Latin census, a poll-tax of a denarius a head assessed on the whole population and remitted by the publicans to the Roman treasury, and because it was a direct personal tax the zealous felt it a deeper humiliation than customs duties and resisted it, as Judas of Galilee did, when they would have paid the others. Barnes, Ellicott and Wesley all set out the dilemma the same way and in the same terms: say the tribute is unlawful and the Herodians denounce him to the governor as an enemy of Caesar; say it is lawful and the Pharisees denounce him to the people as a betrayer of his country’s liberty. Ellicott adds that the second charge was in fact laid against him in the end, in the words about perverting the nation and forbidding to give tribute. Chrysostom judges that of the two they would rather have had him offend the Herodians, since men had already been put to death on that charge as plotting rebellion against the Romans, and that is the suspicion they were angling to bring on him.

Gill notes that the three evangelists between them call the thing wickedness, craftiness and hypocrisy, and that it was all three at once; the mask could not screen them from one who judged not by the outward appearance. Calvin makes the same point the other way round, and turns it into evidence. They had opened the conversation so well that they looked like nothing but excellent scholars; whence then had Christ this knowledge? Not by human conjecture, but because his Spirit is a discerner of hearts, so that before answering at all he exhibited a proof of his divinity by laying their concealed malice open. Since wicked men use snares of the same kind every day and their inward malice is hidden from us, he draws a prayer out of it: that Christ would bestow on us by free gift the spirit of discernment he had by nature and by right, since without that prudence we shall constantly leave the doctrine of God exposed to calumny. Barnes makes the same inference into a doctrinal one, that no mere man can discern the motives of others, so that the verse proves Christ omniscient, and glosses tempt as an attempt to lead him into difficulty by an insidious question. On the name he gives them, Barnes says a hypocrite here is a dissembler professing to be a candid inquirer; Ellicott specifies the form the hypocrisy took, that they came not avowedly as disputants but, in Luke’s phrase, as just men perplexed in conscience and seeking guidance from one they honoured; Wesley puts it in four words, pretending a scruple of conscience.
19:
The coin is identified with care. Gill says the demand is not for money in general but for the currency in which the tribute was actually paid, which was Roman, and values the penny at sevenpence halfpenny. Robertson gives the technical terms: the word behind tribute is the Latin census, a head-tax for which silver denarii were struck bearing Caesar’s figure and superscription, while the word behind money occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and comes from a verb meaning sanctioned by law or custom. Clarke and Barnes both distinguish this from the temple due. Barnes notes that the tribute for the temple service was paid in the Jewish shekel and that for the Roman government in foreign coin, and draws the sharpest inference in the passage: that they carried and used this coin was proof that they themselves held it lawful to pay the tribute, so their pretended scruple was hypocrisy on its face. Clarke makes the same distinction and adds the arithmetic, that the poll tax of the law was half a shekel, roughly twice the denarius, so that what is demanded here is plainly the Roman levy and not the sacred shekel for the repairs of the temple. Ellicott observes from the parable of the labourers that the denarius was in common circulation, suspects a fiscal regulation requiring the poll-tax to be paid in that coin only, and states the consequence: wherever it passed current it was a witness that the independence of the country had gone and that Caesar was its real ruler in temporal things. Calvin builds his whole reading on that. Calling for a coin looks like a small thing, but it is enough to break the snare, because in using it they had already acknowledged subjection; the authority of Rome stood approved by general practice, so Christ had no need to enjoin anything new. The Jews, he says, had voluntarily come under obligation to pay, having given up to the Romans the power of the sword, and it was idle to make a separate dispute of the tribute when the question depended on the general arrangements of the government.

On the image, the numismatics and the politics are handled separately. Barnes explains that the likeness of the reigning prince was struck on coins as it still is on European ones, and that the superscription is the emperor’s name and titles; Ellicott prefers inscription to superscription and takes the coin for a silver denarius of Tiberius with the head on the face and the titles running round it. Robertson adds the local history: the earlier Herods avoided portraits because of Jewish prejudice, the tetrarch Philip introduced them on Jewish coins and Herod Agrippa followed him, but this particular coin was almost certainly struck at Rome with the image and name of Tiberius. Gill supplies only the gesture, the penny held in one hand and pointed at with the other. Clarke reads the question as strategy: Christ knew perfectly whose the image was, and asked in order to make them answer to their own confusion, so that men who came to ensnare him were ensnared themselves — he who digs a pit for his neighbour ordinarily falls into it. Lightfoot alone names what they were fishing for. They wanted to know whether Christ held the opinion of Judas of Galilee, taken up by the men Josephus everywhere calls zealots, who stiffly refused obedience and tribute to a Roman prince because they had persuaded themselves that submission to a heathen government was sin; what that fury cost the nation, he says, both Josephus and the ruins of Jerusalem still testify. His summary is bitter: they chose Caesar before Christ, and because in the end they would have neither Caesar nor Christ they remain a monument to all ages of the divine vengeance and of their own madness.
21:
The answer is read by everyone as drawn out of the questioners’ own admission. Clarke states the chain: you acknowledge the coin to be Caesar’s, it is current in your land, its currency shows the country under Roman government, and your acknowledgment proves you have submitted — so be neither unjust nor impious, but render what you own to be his and God’s to God. Wesley turns the point into an address to both parties present, telling the Pharisees to render Caesar what they themselves acknowledge to be his, and the Herodians, zealous for Caesar as they are, to render God what is God’s. Robertson notes the verb is give back what is already Caesar’s. Gill notes that an Augustan piece inscribed after the taking of Judaea would itself testify to their subjection, and that the rabbis knew the coin as a Caesarean penny.

What the second half of the sentence requires divides them by degrees. Barnes offers two readings without choosing: the annual due for the temple service, so that paying Caesar did not discharge them from paying God, or their hearts, lives, property and influence together. Clarke takes the answer for a settlement of jurisdictions distinguishing the two empires of heaven and earth, and finds the principle in the images: the prince’s image on the coin shows that temporal things belong to his government, and the image of God stamped on the soul that all its faculties belong to the Most High. Hilary reasons in the same figure but makes it conditional: if nothing of Caesar’s remains with us we owe him nothing, but if we use the protection of his power we cannot call it wrong to be required to pay; God’s due is body, soul and will, so give Caesar your money and keep for God a conscience void of offence. Calvin draws a clear distinction between spiritual and civil government, framed against a specific error: some thought they could not be God’s people unless free of every human yoke, and the answer tells us that outward subjection leaves the conscience free before God. Ellicott agrees the reply was in substance an affirmative, since accepting the coinage admitted the emperor’s sovereignty in fact, but says the second clause lifts the matter into another region, and states the wider rule: secular authority claims obedience as an ordinance of God until it encroaches on conscience and prevents men from serving him. Chrysostom sets the limit more bluntly: only such things are meant as are in no way opposed to religion, since anything else is no longer Caesar’s tribute but the Devil’s. Origen takes the saying morally instead: the body is to have its necessaries as a tribute, and what leads to virtue is to be offered to God. Those who press the law without moderation and forbid all care for the body are the Pharisees, forbidding to marry and commanding to abstain from meats; those who indulge the body are the Herodians; and the Saviour would have neither virtue enfeebled by the flesh nor the flesh crushed by it.

On the effect, all who comment agree that both parties lost. Barnes observes that although the decision looked like a verdict for the Herodians, it confounded both sides and prevented the use they meant to make of it, so they retired covered with shame. Ellicott spells out why: the Herodians could not charge him with forbidding the tribute, and the Pharisees found the duty of giving God his own pressed as hard as they had ever pressed it, so they changed tactics and fell back on another plan. Gill notes that the advice could neither be gainsaid nor denied to be good. Clarke totals it on three accounts: Caesar is satisfied to the uttermost farthing, God is glorified, the people edified. Calvin generalises: God turns his enemies’ attempts to another purpose and drives them back with disgrace.
23:
That a second party should step forward the same day, after the first was routed, is what most of them remark on. Chrysostom says the overthrow of their predecessors ought to have held them back, but presumption is shameless and ready to attempt the impossible, and the evangelist notes the day as if wondering at the folly. Pseudo-Chrysostom suspects a competition, a strife over which should be first to seize him, and adds that if argument would not overcome him they hoped perseverance might wear out his understanding. Clarke puts it in a sentence: malice is ever active and however often defeated returns to the charge, because Jesus and his gospel give no quarter to vice and the vicious give none to him. Henry calls it an hour of temptation, with Satan busier than ever to disturb him. Calvin makes the alliance itself the lesson. Deadly strife existed between the two sects, at war with each other daily, yet they conspire against Christ, so that the Pharisees are not sorry to see their own doctrine of the resurrection attacked in his person; and he draws the parallel bluntly, that men who hate the gospel will gladly use Epicureans and Libertines if it serves to destroy it.

Who the Sadducees were is supplied from several directions. Jerome gives the pair of names and finds both pretentious: the Pharisees claimed a righteousness of traditions and were called the separate, while Sadducee is interpreted righteous, they too passing for what they were not. On the doctrine he cites the Acts: where the Pharisees believed the resurrection of body and soul and confessed both angel and spirit, these denied the whole list. Barnes presses the consequence: they denied not only the raising of the body but a future state and the soul’s separate existence, and since the two doctrines stand or fall together our Lord’s answer respects both — though he judges it bears more on the soul and a future state of rewards than on the body. Henry supplies the party’s history: they took their name from one Sadoc, a disciple of Antigonus Sochaeus some two hundred and eighty-four years before Christ’s birth; their own nation’s writers censure them heavily as men of base and debauched life, which he takes to follow from their principles; they were the fewest of the sects but generally persons of rank; and where the Pharisees and Essenes seemed to him to follow Plato, the Sadducees were much of the genius of the Epicureans. Lightfoot preserves their own form of the argument, that the cloud fails and passes away and so he who goes down to the grave does not return, and remarks that this is the reasoning of those who deny infant baptism, the law making no express mention of a resurrection. He also revises his earlier guess: he had suspected the Sadducees of being the Herodians, that is courtiers, but these were of a more inferior sort.

Gill notes that the question was a knotty one with which they had often puzzled the Pharisees, and that they hoped to nonplus Christ with it and expose the absurdity of a doctrine they denied. Pseudo-Chrysostom sees a strategy behind the sect itself. The Devil, unable to crush the religion of God outright, brought in a party denying the resurrection, and so broke down the whole purpose of a righteous life — for who would endure a daily struggle against himself, he asks, unless he looked to that hope? Chrysostom explains why the levirate law existed at all: because death seemed an unmixed evil to a people who lived wholly for the present, Moses ordered that a childless man’s widow be given to his brother, so that a son might be raised to the dead man and his name not perish. It had to be a kinsman, or the child would not have counted as the dead man’s.
24:
They open by citing Moses, and Calvin asks why, since the bare fact would have served. The name is used cunningly, to establish that these were lawful marriages contracted not by the will of men but by God’s own command and appointment; and since God cannot contradict himself, the sophistry runs that if he will one day gather believers into his kingdom and restore what he gave them here, the woman assigned to seven husbands becomes an absurdity. That, he says, is how ungodly men forge their calumnies, to disfigure sound doctrine and shame Christ’s servants, which is why Paul requires a teacher to be armed against adversaries of the truth. On the law itself Barnes and Clarke agree closely: it stands in Deuteronomy, its purpose was to keep the families and tribes of Israel distinct and perpetuate them, and to raise up seed means that the children of such a marriage were reckoned in the genealogy of the dead brother and counted his for all civil purposes. Clarke adds that the word rendered seed should always be translated children or posterity, and that a law precisely similar exists among the Hindoos. Robertson works on the verb, which occurs here alone in the New Testament and elsewhere only in the Greek Old Testament, used generally of persons connected by marriage but specifically, in the story of Judah and in Deuteronomy, of marrying a brother’s widow. Gill notes only that the title they give him is the usual Rabbi.

Whether the case ever happened, none of them can say, and none of them think it matters much. Gill locates the family in whatever town the questioners lived in, probably Jerusalem, notes that the brethren must be brothers on the father’s side since those related only through the mother were not bound by this law, and says outright that whether the case is feigned or real is of no consequence; he adds the rabbinic rule that the widow waited ninety days before the next marriage, to see whether she was with child by the first. Barnes takes it as constructed rather than remembered: they stated a case as difficult as they could make it, and though no such thing may ever have occurred it was at least supposable. Clarke says the same more sharply, that the number seven was raised merely to make the question harder, and Wesley calls the story a kind of commonplace objection which they no doubt produced on every occasion. Robertson agrees and quotes the judgment that they were aiming at amusement rather than deadly mischief, an old conundrum with which they had discomfited the Pharisees before.

What the difficulty really rests on is where they divide. Barnes locates it in an assumption: the Sadducees supposed that substantially the same state of things obtains in the other world as in this, that husbands and wives must be reunited there, and on that footing they could not see how one woman should be wife to seven men. Clarke treats the assumption as a moral symptom rather than an intellectual mistake. The question is well suited to the mouth of a libertine; men who live without God have no other god than the world, and those who lack the happiness of enjoying God have no pleasure but appetite, so that the stream cannot rise higher than its spring — and a paradise built on that principle, he observes, is what Mohammed offered. He also reports the rabbinic answer to the puzzle, that a woman who has had two husbands in this world will have the first only restored to her in the world to come. Gill notices a small textual witness to the questioners’ own position: one version renders the clause hypothetically, if therefore the dead will be raised, which is exactly right, since they were supposing the resurrection for the sake of argument and not granting it.
29:
The answer names two causes of the error, and every commentator follows the division. Ellicott observes that this is the one place in the Gospels where our Lord comes into direct collision with the Sadducees, and that his tone, while condemning their error outright, is less stern than what he keeps for the Pharisees, hypocrisy being the worse corruption of the better thing. The causes he states as an imperfect knowledge even of the Scriptures the Sadducees acknowledged, and imperfect conceptions of the divine attributes, setting an advance limit on what God could do; hence their inability to conceive any fellowship in the risen life but one reproducing this. Barnes adds the observation that gives it force: enemies of the truth make a doctrine of the Bible ridiculous by adding to it and then calling the addition absurd, for nothing in the Scriptures taught that men would marry there. He notes too why the proof is drawn from Moses rather than the clearer passages in Daniel and Isaiah: the questioners had appealed to Moses, and Christ met them on their own ground. Gill says the case was idle and impertinent and our Lord answered it anyway, to expose their ignorance, noting that Mark puts the words as a question. Wesley reduces it to a line: the Scriptures plainly assert a resurrection and the power of God is well able to effect it — how many errors flow from the same source?

Calvin generalises the first cause. Though addressed to the Sadducees the reproof applies to every inventor of false doctrine, since God makes his will clearly known in the Scriptures and ignorance of them is the cause of all errors — which he turns into a consolation, that the godly stay safe so long as they inquire humbly. Why the second cause is joined to the first he also explains: the resurrection so far exceeds the senses that it stays incredible until the mind rises to God’s boundless power; men who measure the heavenly life by the present state have stopped thinking. Clarke locates the deception further back, in the passions, and quotes the rabbis against them on their own ground: those who say the resurrection cannot be proved out of the law are listed among men who shall have no part in the world to come. Origen turns the first cause into a difficulty. If they err by not knowing the Scriptures, is the saying that they neither marry nor are given in marriage written in some Scripture, though not read in the Old Testament? The words are not there, he answers, but their truth is implied in the moral sense, the law being a shadow of good things to come, which when it speaks of husbands and wives speaks chiefly of a spiritual wedlock. He reads the second cause christologically as well: the power they did not know may be Christ himself, unknown to them because they did not know the Scriptures that spoke of him.

What the denial of God’s power amounted to is stated most concretely by three, centuries apart. Barnes supposes they denied, as many have since, that God could gather the scattered dust of the dead and remould it into a body, and calls that setting reason against revelation. Gregory describes the same despair from the inside: men observe the spirit loosed from the body, the flesh turning to corruption and the corruption to dust, the dust resolved into elements beyond the reach of human eyes, and looking on dry bones doubt these can be clothed with flesh again. Augustine answers precisely that objection. The earthy matter of which human flesh is made does not perish before God: reduced to whatever dust, dispersed into whatever vapours, taken up into other bodies, made the food or flesh of animals or of men, it is in a moment restored to the soul that first quickened it.
30:
How far the comparison with the angels reaches is the question, and each draws the line somewhere. Barnes restricts it carefully: the likeness lies in the mode of their existence, and where Luke says they are equal to the angels he means raised above the circumstances of mortality, not equal in intellect. He adds from Luke that they die no more, being children of the resurrection. Calvin restricts it the same way. They will not be like angels in all respects, only so far as they are freed from every infirmity of this life; Luke states the resemblance more exactly, that they can no longer die, from which it follows that there is no propagation of the species. He notes that only believers are in view, the wicked not having been mentioned, and raises a question the others do not. Why say they will then be children of God, when that honour is already given to believers shut up in the frail prison of the body? Because, engrafted by faith into Christ, we are adopted now and may cry Abba, Father, yet since it does not appear what we shall be until we are transformed into his glory, we are not yet actually reckoned his children. Wesley says it in two exclamations: they are incorruptible and immortal, so is the power of God shown in them, so little need of marriage. Gill marks only the moment when bodies and souls are reunited.

Hilary thinks it could have been put more briefly: enough that where the function ceases the empty bodily pleasure ceases too, but Christ adds the angels. He then names the cavil that survives the answer, asking in what form the female sex shall rise; his rule is that whatever Scripture leads us to think of angels we must suppose of women in the resurrection. Augustine comes down for continuity of nature. Those seem to him to judge most justly who do not doubt that both sexes rise; there will be no desire, which is the cause of shame, for before they sinned the first pair were naked, and the nature they then had will be preserved, quit of conception and childbirth, what was in the woman not being adapted to its old use. He also reads the case allegorically: the seven brethren are the wicked, who through the seven ages of this earth brought forth no fruit of righteousness and passed away unfruitful. Dionys describes the state positively rather than by subtraction: when we are incorruptible and immortal we shall be filled by the visible presence of God with most chaste contemplations, and shall share the gift of light to the understanding in an impassible and immaterial soul, after the fashion of the exalted souls in heaven — which is why we are said to be equal to the angels.

Ellicott presses what the doctrine costs. Luke, he notes, sharpens the contrast between the children of this world and the children of the resurrection, and the words teach absolutely that the relations on which marriage rests are absent there. Then he asks the questions that rise as we ponder what lies behind the veil: will there be no continuance of the holiest ties of earth, will husband and wife who loved till death parted them be no more to each other than any others counted worthy of that life, will there be no recognition at all? His answer sends the reader back to the other half of the verse before, the power of God. The old relations may subsist under new conditions, things incompatible here may there co-exist, and the saintly wife of two saintly husbands may love both with an affection angelic and therefore unimpaired. He closes by marking the distance between this and the two things it is most often confused with, the sensual paradise of Mahomet and the dream of earthly marriage merely prolonged.
31:
Why the proof is taken from Exodus rather than from anywhere clearer is settled the same way by three of them. Clarke says the five books were the only Scripture the Sadducees acknowledged as divine, so that confuting them out of those books proved the second half of the charge, that they were ignorant of the very Scriptures they professed to hold sacred; Wesley makes the same point in a sentence. Ellicott lists the places where the hope is expressed more clearly — Job, the Psalms, Daniel — and says our Lord passed them by to meet the Sadducees on their own ground; he notes too that the other Gospels add at the bush, probably naming the section of the law by its title. Gill records the Sadducean position in its own words, that the resurrection cannot be proved out of the law.

The argument itself is stated by each in his own idiom and comes to one thing. Barnes counts the years — Abraham three hundred and twenty-nine dead, Isaac two hundred and twenty-four, Jacob a hundred and ninety-eight — and observes that God still spoke of himself as their God, which would be absurd of a ruler over the annihilated. But he is careful about what is proved: this does not establish the raising of the body directly, only by consequence, since what it establishes is that their souls were alive, and that was the point the Sadducees denied. Clarke reaches the same conclusion and notes that in Sadducean usage death meant eternal annihilation, so that the answer overturns their denial of angel and spirit at the same stroke. Wesley lays the syllogism out formally and adds a small observation on the pronoun, that thy God implies both benefit from God to man and duty from man to God. Ellicott states the principle abstractly: joining the divine name to a man’s asserts a relation existing when the words are spoken and not merely in the past, which is more than saying I am the God whom Abraham once worshipped; and a permanent relation requires a living party to it. Hilary presses the same inference metaphysically. The words were spoken when the patriarchs had long gone to their rest, yet they of whom he was the God must have been in being, for that of which something else is must itself have being; so those who have a God are alive, since God is eternal and the dead cannot possess what is eternal. Raban marks the structure of the reply: on the conditions of the resurrection Christ answered their enquiry, but on the resurrection itself he replies against their unbelief.

Two of them show how old the mode of argument was. Lightfoot points to the Talmudic tractate where the resurrection is maintained out of the law by reasoning not unlike our Saviour’s, and quotes a rabbi who charged the Samaritan scribes with falsehood for denying that it could be so proved, arguing from the sentence that a soul shall be utterly cut off and his iniquity be upon him — cut off in this world, and the iniquity upon him in the world to come. He adds a caution about that passage, that the rabbis there seem to tax the Samaritan text with corruption when in fact both text and version agree well enough with the Hebrew. Cyril of Jerusalem uses this very verse against the same opponents and on the same ground: the Samaritans receive the law only and admit no prophets, so a text from Ezekiel has no force with them, and one must go to the writings of the law, where God says to Moses that he is the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob — which must mean of those who have being and subsistence.
33:
On the astonishment, Remigius makes the small point that it was the multitudes and not the Sadducees who were amazed, and turns it into a pattern of what happens daily in the Church, when the adversaries are overcome by divine inspiration and the faithful rejoice. Ellicott says the wonder was at the manner rather than the matter: the popular creed had been proved from words that to a careless reader seem remote from it, and he notes that the other Gospels record agreement as well as surprise, since the better sort of Pharisees were glad to hear their opponents refuted with a dexterity beyond their ablest scribes. Robertson finds continued amazement in the tense, the crowds being literally struck out of themselves. Wesley says they marvelled at the clearness and solidity of the answers, and Gill guesses that the Sadducees had puzzled many with this question before and never met their match. Clarke draws the general moral: God uses the infidelity of some for the edification of others, and had no false doctrine ever been broached we should never have seen the full evidence of the true, for truth always gains by being opposed.

The verb for what had been done to the Sadducees is noticed by two. Ellicott says its primary sense is to stop a man’s power of speech with a gag, and that even in wider use it keeps the note of a silence imposed and unwilling; Robertson renders it bluntly as muzzled, and observes that the Pharisees could not restrain their glee at it even while they were joining the same Sadducees in the attempt to entrap Jesus. On the gathering, Clarke reports that the phrase means they came together with one accord or for one purpose, and that some copies read outright against him; Robertson borrows a modern version’s phrase and says they mustered their forces. Barnes leaves the motive open between rejoicing that their rivals had been confounded and laying a fresh plan, and thinks both were true, since they would look for the hardest question in dispute among themselves and try it on him. Gill supposes they heard of the defeat at second hand, from the scribes who had approved the answer, the Pharisees themselves having withdrawn earlier with the Herodians. Henry is harshest on the motive: they gathered not to thank him for defending against the Sadducees a truth of their own religion, but to win the credit of puzzling the man who had puzzled them, being more vexed that Christ was honoured than pleased that their rivals were silenced, and more concerned for their own traditions than for the resurrection itself — which he makes a standing instance of the envy that is displeased at a confessed truth when the wrong person maintains it, and sacrifices a public good to a private grudge, where Paul was otherwise minded. Jerome says the same in a sentence: they had been confuted already over the denarius and had just watched their adversaries overthrown, and should have taken warning, but hate and jealousy are the parents of impudence, and two parties at enmity with each other unite for this. John Chrysostom marks the same boldness, that men who ought to have held their peace at such a moment press their former attempt instead, and adds a guess at their calculation: since the first commandment is to love God, they expected him to amend it in order to show that he too was God, and so to give them a handle.
35:
The title given to the questioner is glossed by four of them. Barnes warns that lawyer does not mean a practitioner as with us but a man learned in the law of Moses, and that Mark’s scribe means the same; Clarke agrees that the rendering conveys a wrong idea and prefers teacher of the law, suggesting that these letter-men were the Karaites, who rejected the traditions of the elders and admitted nothing but the written word, and are allowed to have kept closer to its spiritual meaning than the Pharisees did — which is why he thinks this question more refined than any before it. Ellicott says the distinction between lawyer and scribe rested on technicalities that have left little trace, and guesses at a section of the scribes who confined themselves to the Law while others took in the Prophets, noting that Luke keeps lawyers distinct from Pharisees. Gill collects the versions and concludes that lawyers and scribes were one and the same, this man being a Pharisee by sect and a scribe by office. On his motive, Ellicott, Wesley and Barnes incline to acquit him: the word for tempting need not imply hostility and is used elsewhere of trying or examining, Wesley thinks he meant no ill design but a further trial of the wisdom that had silenced the Sadducees, and Barnes reckons him candid, acting as the party’s agent without sharing its malice; Ellicott suspects the refutation of the Sadducees had drawn sympathy from minds not hardened in hypocrisy.

Pseudo-Chrysostom reads the tactics of the meeting itself. They assemble so that numbers may silence the man their reasoning could not confute, which is itself a confession that truth had failed them; and one shall speak for all and all through one, so that a victory may belong to the party and a defeat rest on the single speaker. Of the speaker he observes that a man who asks after the greatest commandment had not kept the least, and that only one who has fulfilled the lower righteousness should seek the higher. Origen takes the silencing of the Sadducees for a principle: the tongue of falsehood is silenced by the brightness of truth, and as it belongs to a righteous man to be silent when silence is good and to speak when speech is good, so a teacher of lies is silent so far as any good purpose is concerned. He then turns the lawyer into a type. Everyone who questions a teacher to try him rather than learn of him is this Pharisee’s brother, and the address Master convicts him, since none but a disciple would use it: whoever calls the Word his master without learning from it stands in the same place. He suspects too that the question was a standing one among them before Christ came.

Whether the questioner was sincere is disputed, and the dispute turns on Mark. Augustine sees no difficulty in Matthew saying the man came to tempt while Mark ends with Christ telling him he is not far from the kingdom of God: either he came to tempt and the answer wrought correction in him, or the tempting meant is not an enemy’s design to deceive but the cautious approach of a man making proof of a stranger, since he who believes lightly is of a vain heart. Calvin reaches the opposite conclusion by comparing Luke instead. All the accounts agree that the question was put to tempt, but the man in Matthew and Mark goes away with no bad disposition, acquiesces in the reply and shows a teachable and gentle mind, whereas Luke’s enquirer is obstinate and swelled with pride and gives no sign of repentance; so Calvin judges that the narratives only resemble each other and are probably not the same event, though he does not press the point to a dispute.
36:
What the question meant to a scribe is filled in by the rest. Barnes reports that the Jews divided the law into greater and smaller commandments without ever settling which was greatest, some naming sacrifice, some circumcision, some the washings. Robertson supplies the count they worked with — two hundred and forty-eight affirmative precepts, as many as the members of the body, and three hundred and sixty-five negative, as many as the days of the year, six hundred and thirteen in all, the number of letters in the Decalogue — and says Jesus cuts straight through such hair-splitting to the heart of the matter. Gill narrows what is being asked: not whether the oral law outranks the written, though the Jews gave the preference to tradition, but a question about the written law of Moses, and not merely about the decalogue or whether the first table outranks the second or affirmative precepts the negative, but about the whole body of the law, moral and ceremonial together. Ellicott notes that the Greek asks literally of what kind, as though the commandment belonged to a class, where our Lord’s answer is definite. Clarke closes the series of attacks by sorting them: the Herodians, politicians and courtiers, framed their question on the rights of the prince and matters of state; the Sadducees framed theirs on articles of faith they did not themselves credit; and the Pharisees and their lawyers framed theirs on the very practical godliness of which they wished to be thought the sole proprietors.

Gill adds the rabbinic sentence that stands behind the difficulty, that the Jews themselves reckoned the affirmative precepts weightier than the negative and the first table weightier than the second, so that a lawyer could put the question in good faith and expect a school answer rather than a verse. Barnes makes the same point from the other side, that the division into greater and lesser was universally granted and only the ranking was open, which is why the question was thought hard enough to be worth trying on him. Clarke, for his part, notes that this last party chose the ground most flattering to itself, the love of God and man, of which its members wished to be thought the sole proprietors.
37:
Three of them begin where Mark begins, with the confession of one God prefixed to the commandment. Barnes says the reason is that all true obedience depends on a correct knowledge of God, since no one keeps commandments who does not know the nature and perfections and right of the one commanding. Ellicott makes the same structural point, that the creed of Israel stands in its right place as the foundation of the duty, and adds two observations: the answer comes from the very chapter that supplied two of the three replies to the Tempter, and it repeats what a lawyer had himself given on an earlier occasion — from which he draws a concession, that in their ethical teaching the Pharisees had grasped the truth intellectually even while failing to live it, and that our Lord did not shrink from identifying his teaching with theirs, truth being truth even when coupled with hypocrisy. Calvin finds two supports for the law’s authority in the same preface. It is a powerful excitement to worship to know that the one we worship is the actual Creator, since doubt breeds indifference; and it is a gentle inducement that he freely adopts us as his people, so that distrust may not hold us back. The same words, he adds, distinguish God from every idol.

What the three clauses mean is where they separate, and the divisions do not line up. Barnes reads heart as the affections fixed on God more strongly than on anything else and ready to surrender whatever we hold dear at his command, soul as life itself, a readiness to live for him and die at his word, and mind as the intellect submitted, loving his law above the decisions of our own minds. Clarke divides the same way at greater length, including the fourth clause Mark supplies: with all the heart is to love nothing in comparison of God and nothing but in reference to him, holding no hope or fear except as regulated by him; with all the soul is to be ready to give up life, from which principle sprang the blood of the martyrs; with all the strength is to spare neither labour nor cost and to spend time, health, ease and goods in that service; with all the mind is to study nothing but as it serves God and to banish every useless or defiling thought. He prefaces the whole with the word itself, canvassing four proposed derivations of the Greek and settling on a definition — a sovereign preference given to one above all others, a concentration of every thought and desire upon a single object. Augustine assigns the clauses differently: the heart is our whole thought, the soul our whole life, the mind our whole understanding, and the point of the threefold demand is that no part of our life is left which may justly be unfilled of him or given over to enjoying some other final good. Gloss differs from all of them, making the heart the understanding, the soul the will and the mind the memory, so that a man shall think and will and remember nothing contrary to God.

Pseudo-Chrysostom fastens on the verb rather than the faculties. It is love and not fear, and to love is more than to fear, since fear belongs to slaves and love to sons, fear lies in compulsion and love in freedom; whoever serves God in fear escapes punishment but does not gain the reward of righteousness. John Chrysostom reads the choice of commandment as a diagnosis of the questioners, who were led to ask precisely because they had no charity, pining with envy and seized by jealousy. Gill notes that the answer came directly, and that Christ gave it although he knew the design behind the question, since it would instruct the people as well as silence his adversaries.
38: On its rank, Gill calls it first in order of nature, time, dignity and causality, God being the first cause of all things and love to him the spring of love to a neighbour, and greatest in its object, nature, manner and end. Barnes agrees that first means first in importance and not in time, calls it the fountain of all the rest, and grounds the whole in a principle of proportion: all beings are to be loved according to their excellence, and God being the most excellent is to be loved supremely, after which our affections will fall rightly on everything else. Clarke sets out ten grounds for its primacy, among them its antiquity, being as old as the world and engraven on our nature; its justice, since it alone renders God his due; its sufficiency, being of itself able to make men holy here and happy hereafter; its extent, leaving nothing to the creature that it does not refer to the Creator; and its duration, never to be discontinued in heaven. Gill presses the same from three sides at once — the object of the command, God being the first and chief good; the manner of it, since it engrosses the whole heart, soul, mind and strength; and its function, being the principle from which all duties flow and the end to which all are referred — and notes that the Jews themselves could not deny how comprehensive the words are. Barnes adds that it is greatest in dignity, in excellence, in extent and in duration. Among Clarke’s remaining grounds are its dignity, as proceeding directly from God and referring directly to him; its excellence, as the commandment of the new covenant and the very spirit of the divine adoption; its fruitfulness, as the root of all commandments and the fulfilling of the law; its virtue and efficacy, since by this alone God reigns in the heart of man and man is united to God; and its sheer necessity, being a thing absolutely indispensable. He is careful too that its duration runs both ways, ever to be continued on earth and never to be discontinued in heaven, so that of all commands this is the one which death does not suspend and glory does not supersede.
39:
That the second is like the first is taken by everyone to mean more than that it stands next. Gill points out that there is a second and no third, which is itself a reduction against the six hundred and thirteen the scribes counted, and explains the likeness by what the two demand rather than by whom they concern: the object differs, but the same true, hearty, sincere love is required, always and towards all, and it must spring from love to God and be done to his glory. Barnes says it resembles the first in importance, dignity, purity and usefulness, notes that the lawyer had not asked for it and that Christ volunteered it in order to give him the substance of the whole law, and adds from Mark that no commandment is greater than these, none concerning circumcision or sacrifice included. Hilary reads the likeness as an equality of obligation and of merit, and gives a reason that goes past ethics: no love of God without Christ, and no love of Christ without God, can profit to salvation. Ellicott finds it worth remarking where the words come from — a book that is for the most part pre-eminently ceremonial — and gives the Pharisees credit as ethical teachers for having drawn the sentence out of its obscurity and set it second only to the first, exactly as our Lord now does. Raban maps the pair onto the decalogue, the first table belonging to the love of God and the second to the love of our neighbour.

Calvin argues the dependence in both directions. The order matters, worship of God standing first, because until the love of God reigns there will never be true charity towards men: what the children of this world feel for one another is not real love but a mercenary love, since every one of them has an eye to his own advantage. And the converse holds as strictly, for it is impossible that the love of God should reign without producing brotherly kindness. He also refuses a scholastic use of the measure: when Moses said as thyself he did not put self-love first in such a way that a man must love himself before loving his neighbour, as the schoolmen cavil when they insist that a rule must always come before what it measures. Clarke describes the second love by its content: a love of equity, charity, succour and benevolence, which owes to a neighbour what we have a right to expect from him, and which is regulated by the positive command to do to all men as we would they should do to us.
