From that rule he draws practical directions — to put the best construction that words and actions will bear, to bear with and forgive, to rejoice in another’s felicity and mourn in his adversity, to instruct his ignorance and help his weakness and risk life itself for his sake and for the public good — and he grounds the whole in the first command, love of neighbour springing from love of God as its source and returning as its infallible mark.
40: On the closing sentence they are careful about what is and is not being claimed. Gill denies that everything in Moses and the prophets is reducible to these two, since much is promise and much is history, and limits the claim to the preceptive part: whatever concerns duty is summarily comprehended here, and the prophets, as to their precepts, are an enlargement of the law. Calvin makes the identical restriction and states why it matters: a distinction must be kept between the promises and the commandments, so those are mistaken who read the saying as though nothing higher were to be sought in Scripture, since Christ is not describing everything we learn from the word of God but the end to which all the commandments tend. Ellicott says the two were the root and the rest expanded and applied them, or set them forth symbolically in the ceremonial, or, as in the laws of slavery and divorce, confined their application within limits that the hardness of men’s hearts made necessary. Barnes puts it plainly, that love to God and man comprehends the whole of religion and that to produce it was the design of Moses, the prophets, the Saviour and the apostles; and he follows the scene to its end from Mark, where the scribe assents that this is more than all burnt offerings and sacrifices and is told that he is not far from the kingdom of God. Clarke gives the image for the structure: the two are the first and last links of a chain on which all the intermediate ones depend, uniting God to man, man to his fellows, and men again to God, since true religion begins and ends in love; and he grounds the claim on Paul, that love is the fulfilling of the law, because whoever has the love of God in him delights to obey the divine precepts and to do all manner of kindness to men for God’s sake. Gill supports the same from the rabbinic side, citing the saying that all the prophets stood on Mount Sinai and received their prophecies there, on the ground that the sum of them, so far as duty goes, was delivered then; the prophets, in their preceptive part, are an enlargement upon the law rather than an addition to it. Ellicott notes that the two nouns are coupled here as they are earlier in this Gospel to stand for the whole revelation of the divine will in the Old Testament, so that nothing is left outside the claim.
41: The turn of the questioning is remarked by all of them. Barnes says Christ, having confounded the great sects in succession, now takes his turn, and lists three purposes for it: to show them how ignorant they were of their own prophecies, to humble them for that ignorance, and to bring forward the true doctrine of a Messiah whose character is higher than David’s, being David’s Lord at the same time as his descendant. Clarke says the same more briefly, that the source of all the captious questions put to him that day was ignorance of the prophecies about the Messiah. Ellicott notes that the other Gospels place here the remark Matthew keeps for the end, that no man dared ask him any more questions, and that from this point the opposition abandons argument for treachery and false witness; it was now his turn to be the questioner, and to convict them of resting on the mere surface of the predictions they quoted most confidently. Gill is careful about the timing, that the Pharisees were still gathered about him and had not yet left, their own doctor having been answered and having nothing more to say. Henry makes the same point with relish: he did not take one of them apart from the rest but faced them all together, in confederacy and at their strongest, which he takes for God’s manner — to give his enemies every advantage they could wish and conquer them anyway. Raban draws a short moral from the whole encounter, that the poison of jealousy may be overcome but can hardly of itself rest at peace. Origen adds a note on the form of the question: had their asking sprung from a desire to know, Christ would never have put to them something framed to deter them from asking further. Henry sets the reversal in a sentence: many questions the Pharisees had asked him, by which, though they thought to pose him, they did but expose themselves, and now it is his turn to ask one — and he hears behind it the prophet’s warning that men may associate themselves and yet be broken in pieces. He notes as well that the question Christ chose was one they could easily answer, being a question out of their own catechism.
42:
What the question asks, and what it does not, is where the moderns are most exact. Barnes insists that Christ did not ask their views of himself, his person and his work, as our translation may suggest, but their views of the Messiah, and specifically of his genealogy; and he notes that the definite article should have been kept, so that the word reads as a title and not a name. Robertson says the same, that this is the Messiah and not a proper name of Jesus, and observes that Jesus here assumes the psalm to be Messianic and by the question touches the problem of his own person, his deity and his humanity together, which the Pharisees had probably never faced. Clarke keeps the article too and turns the answer into an argument the Jews of his own day must meet: descent from David was universally acknowledged and undisputed, yet their families are now so confounded that no genealogy can be traced with any certainty, and none has been for sixteen hundred years; if the Messiah was so often and so expressly promised from that family, why should he appear only after the public registers were destroyed, unless God meant him to come while they could still be inspected? Ellicott finds the exchange sharpened by its timing, since the crowd had shouted that very title in the Hosannas a few days before, and observes that the Pharisees produce the traditional answer at once without ever having asked whether it was the whole truth or how it squares with predictions they themselves grant to be Messianic. Gill widens the question’s reach: not whether such a person was coming, which they never doubted, but what they thought of him — whether divine or merely human, whether the salvation he brings is spiritual or temporal, whether his kingdom is of this world, and above all whose son he is.

Three read the answer as the mark of a settled error. Chrysostom observes that Christ asked his disciples what others said of him and then what they themselves said, but does not do that here, since these would have called him a deceiver; they held the Messiah to be mere man, and that is why they answer as they do, so he produces the prophet as a witness to his dominion, his proper sonship, and his joint honour with the Father. Pseudo-Chrysostom reads the motive behind the indirection: Christ wished to show that he knew the treachery of their hearts and that he was God, but would not say it plainly lest they charge him with blasphemy, nor conceal it, since he had come to preach the truth, and so he framed a question that would tell them who he was. He adds that the question serves against more than Pharisees, since according to the flesh Christ was truly David’s son and according to his Godhead David’s Lord. Calvin puts the same diagnosis historically. Because God had so often promised that Christ would come of that family, the conviction was rooted too deep for Satan to attack directly, so he let the Messiah be acknowledged as a true man and a son of David and stripped him instead of his divinity, leaving him one ordinary descendant of Adam among others — by which the hope of eternal life and of spiritual righteousness was abolished. Ever since, he adds, heretics have worked underground at the same task from one side or the other.
43:
What the argument assumes is set out most fully by Ellicott: that David wrote the psalm, that in writing it he was guided by a Spirit higher than his own, and that its subject was no earthly king of David’s house but the far-off Christ. On that last point, he says, there was an undisturbed consensus among the schools of Judaism as the Targums and the Talmud represent them, with a received tradition that the Christ should sit at the right hand of Jehovah and Abraham on his left; and the Messianic application is claimed by Peter, indirectly by Paul, and given well-nigh the chief place in the argument of the Epistle to the Hebrews. The only hypothesis on which another meaning could be assigned is that the psalm was written not by David but of him. He then tracks the sequence: the words show Jehovah speaking to David’s Adonai as the true anointed king, and if that is the title, must its bearer not be more than a son of David by natural descent — and were scribes who had never so much as asked themselves the question not self-convicted of incompetence as religious teachers? Barnes puts the same question with one careful limitation. Lord here means superior, not necessarily divine: David calls him his superior, master and lawgiver. But if the Messiah were merely a descendant, having a human nature only and no existence when the psalm was written, with what propriety could David call him Lord? Wesley reduces it to two clauses, and Clarke and Barnes agree that in spirit means by the inspiration of the Spirit, David speaking as a prophet. Gill notes that Christ does not deny what they said but grants it, arguing on their own answer while tacitly refusing the sense they put on it.

Calvin makes the emphasis fall on that same phrase and explains what it forecloses. By saying David spoke in the Spirit, Christ contrasts a prediction of something future with testimony to something present, and so anticipates the escape by which the psalm is referred to David’s own reign, as though it merely celebrated a king who would rise above the mad attempts of his enemies. The psalm itself refutes that, since it introduces a king clothed with a new priesthood by which the ancient shadows of the law must be abolished, which fits no earthly king at all. He does not pretend the argument is beyond objection, and states the objection himself: it might be said that David, composing the psalm for the people to sing and not with any view to his own person, was simply assigning to Christ a dominion over others. Jerome reports the evasions actually offered. Those who look for a Christ still to come make him a mere man, however holy, of David’s race, and to escape the question they allege Abraham’s steward and say the psalm was composed in his person, addressed to his lord Abraham after the overthrow of the five kings; Jerome answers by asking how Abraham could say what follows in the psalm. His own account of the title is that Christ is David’s Lord not by descent but by his eternal generation from the Father, in which he was before his fleshly forefather, and that David used the word not by chance or of his own thought but by the Holy Spirit. Cyril of Jerusalem gathers the same psalm into a chain of testimonies to the Son’s sitting at the Father’s right hand, noting that the Saviour himself confirms it here, that Peter cited it in very words at Pentecost, and that Paul returns to it to the Romans, the Ephesians, the Colossians and in the Epistle to the Hebrews.
44: On the two clauses of the quotation the readings are complementary. Gill identifies the speaker as Jehovah the Father and the one addressed as the Messiah, David’s Lord by right of creation and of redemption alike, since as God he made him and as Saviour redeemed him, and dates the saying to the ascension. Clarke glosses the Hebrew words, the second meaning prop or stay or support, and reads the invitation as the place of greatest eminence and authority, with the subduing of Jews and Gentiles alike to follow. Barnes explains the imagery from custom, that a seat at a king’s right hand signified favour, trust and power, and that a footstool is whatever is under the feet of one sitting, so that the enemies are under subjection. Wesley draws the inference that a dominion to which David himself was subject shows both the heavenly majesty of this king and the nature of his kingdom. Remigius warns against the obvious misreading: the right hand does not imply that God has a body, and to sit there is to abide in the honour and equality of the Father’s majesty, while till stands for indefinite time and means sit thou for ever. Gloss forestalls another, that the Father’s putting the enemies under the Son argues no weakness in the Son but the union of his nature with the Father’s, since the Son in turn puts down the Father’s enemies whenever he glorifies that name on earth. Calvin hears in the verse a song of triumph put by the Spirit into the mouth of all the godly, so that when the kingdom is violently attacked they may set an inviolable decree of heaven against every exertion of its adversaries, and he takes the right hand for a metaphor of rank rather than of place, denoting the highest government held in God’s name and embracing heaven and earth together. Origen adds the one note that looks the other way: God puts Christ’s enemies beneath his feet for their salvation as well as for their destruction. Cyril of Jerusalem, pressing the same clause, piles up the apostolic witnesses to the session at the right hand — the Son of Man seen sitting on the right hand of power, Peter writing of one who is at the right hand of God having gone into heaven, Paul to the Romans naming Christ risen and at the right hand of God, to the Ephesians the mighty working that raised him and set him there, to the Colossians the things above where Christ is seated, and the Epistle to the Hebrews on the purification he had made before he sat down.
45:
The force of the closing question is put most fully by Barnes. If the Messiah was David’s Lord, his superior, and if he had an existence at the time the psalm was written, how could he also be descended from him? They could not answer, and Barnes holds there is no way of answering except by admitting the whole of what the question implies: that the Messiah was divine as well as human, that he existed already in David’s day and was his Lord and Master, his God and King, and that as man he was afterwards descended from him. Clarke argues from their silence in the same direction, but by elimination. The Jews did not attempt to deny the conclusion, which shows they could not; the one way of invalidating the argument would have been to deny that the prophecy related to the Messiah at all, and that reading was so fully and generally received among them that no one tried it. Gill notes only that the identification is assumed and that the Pharisees were in no position to deny it. On the silence itself Gill states the dilemma they were caught in: either acknowledge the deity of the Messiah or confess their ignorance, and since they cared to do neither they judged silence the wisest part.

Clarke closes the day with a tally, borrowed in part and in part his own. He quotes the observation that our Lord put the four great sects to silence in one day and in succession — the Herodians and Pharisees on the tribute, the Sadducees on the woman and the seven brethren, then the scribe or Karaite, who owned no authority beyond the written law, on the great commandment — and notes that this last man deserves separate mention, since he not only acquiesced in the answer but commended it. His own summary runs through the same four scenes: the Pharisees and Herodians defeated, the Sadducees confounded, the lawyers nonplussed, and the Pharisees finally routed, so that the wisdom of God triumphed over the cunning of men. He also marks what follows from the exhaustion of their arguments, which is not peace: from this point our Lord is no more troubled with captious questions, their whole stock being spent, and they turn instead to deliberating coolly how he may be got murdered — for a man who resists the truth of God is capable of carrying out the worst purpose of Satan. Wesley adds the one qualification the verse allows, that what ceased was questioning by way of ensnaring and tempting.

Barnes uses the end of the chapter to gather its lessons, and they fall almost entirely on the parable with which it opened. Multitudes who are invited to be saved reject the gospel and perish in their sins; and if they perish, they only are to blame, since the offer was freely made and the salvation provided, and the sole reason they were not saved is that they would not come. Attention to the affairs of this life, and the love of the world, will shut many out of the kingdom — some attention to those things being necessary, but never such as leads to the loss of the soul. To reject the gospel is ingratitude, God having sent his Son to die for us and followed us with mercies, so that refusal is contempt as well as self-condemnation; and he states the point as sharply as it can be put, that a man has no right to be damned and is under the most solemn obligation to be saved. He ends where the highways were swept, observing that many of the poor and needy will be saved while the haughty and the rich perish for ever.
